result:
Both integrate changes from one branch into another; they differ in what they do to history.

**Merge** ties the two branches together with a new merge commit. Existing commits are untouched.

```
A---B---C---F---G  main
         \       \
          D---E---M  feature   (git merge main)
```

**Rebase** replays your commits on top of the other branch, creating new commits with new hashes. History becomes a straight line.

```
A---B---C---F---G  main
                 \
                  D'---E'  feature   (git rebase main)
```

| | Merge | Rebase |
|---|---|---|
| History | Preserved as it happened, with branch points | Linear, rewritten |
| Commit hashes | Unchanged | Changed for replayed commits |
| Conflicts | Resolved once, in the merge commit | Resolved per replayed commit |
| Safe on shared branches | Yes | No |
| Undo | Revert the merge commit | `git reflog` to find the old tip |

**Rule of thumb:**
- Rebase your own local, unpushed work to tidy it up or catch up with `main`.
- Merge when bringing a finished branch into a shared one, or whenever others have already pulled the commits.

Never rebase commits other people have based work on: their history will no longer match yours, and the fix involves a force-push (`--force-with-lease`, never plain `--force`) plus cleanup on their side.
